name: Mewing with nasal breathing only

card.summary: A version of mewing that pairs resting tongue posture with strict nose breathing, aimed at supporting a well-defined jaw and midface.
card.note: Studies link chronic mouth breathing in children to facial form, but none have tested adult tongue posture plus nose breathing for appearance.

quick.overview:
Mewing is a tongue-posture routine named after orthodontist John Mew, in which the tongue rests against the roof of the mouth and the lips stay closed. The nasal-breathing version adds one rule: all breathing, day and night, goes through the nose, with the mouth kept shut.

Practitioners hope this helps the jaw, cheekbones and midface look more defined and keeps the face from looking long or slack. Research does link chronic mouth breathing in growing children with a longer, narrower face, but no published trial has tested whether the combined habit changes the looks of adults.
quick.how: People keep the lips together, rest the tongue on the palate and breathe through the nose through the day, and some use mouth tape at night. It is usually practiced alongside other habits such as upright head posture and chewing. Followers describe it as a long-term habit, with changes reported over months to years.
quick.risks: The habit itself is low-risk. Nose breathing can be difficult for people with chronic nasal obstruction, and mouth taping during sleep has been little studied. Persistent mouth breathing can be a sign of an airway problem worth discussing with a clinician.

lead: Mewing with nasal breathing only is a form of mewing, the oral-posture practice popularised by the British orthodontist John Mew (1928-2025), in which the person rests the whole tongue against the palate with lips closed and breathes exclusively through the nose [1]. The strict nasal-breathing rule reflects the premise that tongue posture and airway function work together on facial development.

Practitioners use it to pursue a more defined jawline, a forward-set midface and a less long-looking face. Proponents say that when the mouth is closed and the tongue sits up, the face is supported from within, while open-mouth breathing lets the tongue drop and the lower face hang [1].

Orthotropics, Mew's system, is described as not supported by professional orthodontists, who attribute crooked teeth and jaw form mainly to genetics [1]. Separate research on chronic mouth breathing in children suggests it may contribute to a long, narrow face, although the direction of cause and effect is debated [2]. No published study has tested nose-only mewing as a looks intervention in adults.

Proponents expect better-supported jaw and midface over time
angle.text: Followers use the habit hoping for a sharper jaw and fuller midface, and a face that looks less long. Nose-only breathing is meant to keep the mouth closed so the tongue can stay in its resting position.

infobox: None (some add mouth tape at night)

paras: The practice combines two habits: a resting tongue posture, with the tongue pressed along the roof of the mouth, and exclusive nasal breathing with closed lips. Mew summarised the posture as standing up straight and keeping the mouth shut [1].
Nasal breathing is also discussed in general medicine. The nose filters, warms and humidifies air and produces nitric oxide, which mouth breathing does not [2].

Mew developed orthotropics in Britain and argued that the tongue's resting position exerts outward force that can widen the upper jaw in a growing child [1]. The term mewing spread online through video creators and forums, where the nasal-breathing rule became part of the commonly shared routine.

Mew was reprimanded by the UK General Dental Council in 2010 over advertising, and his licence was revoked in 2017; his son Michael was later expelled from the British Orthodontic Society for continuing to advocate the approach [1].

Chronic mouth breathing in children is associated with long face syndrome and other dental changes, and reviewers note that a long, narrow facial type may in turn predispose to obstructed nasal breathing [2]. Mouth taping has been little studied [2].
Mainstream orthodontists say orthotropics has plausible elements but inadequate evidence of efficacy and is not an alternative to orthognathic surgery [1].
No studies found. Related research on mouth breathing in children is summarised above [2].

Persistent mouth breathing is often an adaptation to nasal congestion, and mouth breathing is associated with sleep apnea and snoring [2]. People with blocked noses may find strict nasal breathing difficult.
